performed_via_github_app.name: boring-cyborg
performed_via_github_app.description:
A Github bot to automatically label PRs, issues and perform all the boring operations that you don't want to do.


![Using Boring Cyborg Probot to add new labels](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kaxil/boring-cyborg/master/assets/usage-screenshot-1.png)

![Congratulate user on first merged PR](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kaxil/boring-cyborg/master/assets/usage-first-merged-pr.gif)

## Features

* Add labels based on the path of the file that are modified in the PR.
* Welcome new users to your project when they open their first Issue/PR or first merged PR by an
automated comment. 
* Insert Issue (Jira/Github etc) link in PR description based on the Issue ID in PR title.
* Verifies if commits/PR titles match the regular expression specified
* Check if a branch is up to date with the master when specific files are modified in the PR. This is helpful when you desire the changes to be applied sequentially, for example, alembic migrations.

## Usage

1. **[Configure the Github App](https://github.com/apps/boring-cyborg)**
2. After installing the Github app, create `.github/boring-cyborg.yml` in the default branch to enable it
3. It will start scanning for pull requests within few minutes.

```yaml
##### Labeler ##########################################################################################################
# Enable "labeler" for your PR that would add labels to PRs based on the paths that are modified in the PR.
labelPRBasedOnFilePath:
  # Add 'label1' to any changes within 'example' folder or any subfolders
  label1:
    - example/**/*

  # Add 'label2' to any file changes within 'example2' folder
  label2:
    - example2/*

  # Complex: Add 'area/core' label to any change within the 'core' package
  area/core:
    - src/core/*
    - src/core/**/*  

  # Add 'test' label to any change to *.spec.js files within the source dir
  test:
    - src/**/*.spec.js

##### Greetings ########################################################################################################
# Comment to be posted to welcome users when they open their first PR
firstPRWelcomeComment: >
  Thanks for opening this pull request! Please check out our contributing guidelines.

# Comment to be posted to congratulate user on their first merged PR
firstPRMergeComment: >
  Awesome work, congrats on your first merged pull request!

# Comment to be posted to on first time issues
firstIssueWelcomeComment: >
  Thanks for opening your first issue here! Be sure to follow the issue template!

###### IssueLink Adder #################################################################################################
# Insert Issue (Jira/Github etc) link in PR description based on the Issue ID in PR title.
insertIssueLinkInPrDescription:
   # specify the placeholder for the issue link that should be present in the description
  descriptionIssuePlaceholderRegexp: "^Issue link: (.*)$"
  matchers:
    # you can have several matches - for different types of issues
    # only the first matching entry is replaced
    jiraIssueMatch:
      # specify the regexp of issue id that you can find in the title of the PR
      # the match groups can be used to build the issue id (${1}, ${2}, etc.).
      titleIssueIdRegexp: \[(AIRFLOW-[0-9]{4})\]
      # the issue link to be added. ${1}, ${2} ... are replaced with the match groups from the
      # title match (remember to use quotes)
      descriptionIssueLink: "[${1}](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/${1}/)"
    docOnlyIssueMatch:
      titleIssueIdRegexp: \[(AIRFLOW-X{4})\]
      descriptionIssueLink: "`Document only change, no JIRA issue`"

###### Title Validator #################################################################################################
# Verifies if commit/PR titles match the regexp specified
verifyTitles:
  # Regular expression that should be matched by titles of commits or PR
  titleRegexp: ^\[AIRFLOW-[0-9]{4}\].*$|^\[AIRFLOW-XXXX\].*$
  # If set to true, it will always check the PR title (as opposed to the individual commits).
  alwaysUsePrTitle: true
  # If set to true, it will only check the commit in case there is a single commit.
  # In case of multiple commits it will check PR title.
  # This reflects the standard behaviour of Github that for `Squash & Merge` GitHub
  # uses the PR title rather than commit messages for the squashed commit ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
  # For single-commit PRs it takes the squashed commit message from the commit as expected.
  #
  # If set to false it will check all commit messages. This is useful when you do not squash commits at merge.
  validateEitherPrOrSingleCommitTitle: true
  # The title the GitHub status should appear from.
  statusTitle: "Title Validator"
  # A custom message to be displayed when the title passes validation.
  successMessage: "Validation successful!"
  # A custom message to be displayed when the title fails validation.
  # Allows insertion of ${type} (commit/PR), ${title} (the title validated) and ${regex} (the titleRegexp above).
  failureMessage: "Wrong ${type} title: ${title}"

###### PR/Branch Up-To-Date Checker ####################################################################################
# Check if the branch is up to date with master when certain files are modified
checkUpToDate:
  # The default branch is "master", change the branch if you want to check against a different target branch  
  targetBranch: master
  files:
  # File paths that you want to check for
  # In this example, it checks if the branch is up to date when alembic migrations are modified in the PR.
  # It helps avoid multiple heads in alembic migrations in a collaborative development project.
    - airflow/migrations/*
    - airflow/migrations/**/*
    - airflow/alembic.ini
```

All the features are optional. Simply add the config for the feature you want to use.

If you are having issues with the GitHub app not working, please create an issue on https://github.com/kaxil/boring-cyborg/issues.

Hi, I’d like to investigate this issue.

I plan to first reproduce the reported logging performance regression on Airflow 3.2.0 and the current `main` branch. I will then profile the task-logging path to isolate the overhead from formatting, serialization, task-supervisor communication, and persistence.

If the regression is reproducible, I’ll share the benchmark results and proposed approach here before opening a PR, and I’ll include appropriate regression tests with any fix.

Is anyone currently working on this, or is there any maintainer guidance I should consider before starting?

issue.title: Add micro-benchmarks for the task SDK's supervisor comms

repository.description: Apache Airflow - A platform to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor workflows

issue.body:
**Draft, opened to start a discussion on the dev list.** Based on `main`; the measurements below come from a fix on #62922, but the benchmarks do not depend on it.

related: #62922, #74579

#74579 asks agents to measure these paths by hand in the meantime; this PR is the repeatable, automated version of that step.

## Why

Airflow has no automated check on the performance of its hot paths. A change that makes them slower is only noticed when someone happens to measure it by hand, often after a release: #71721 reports structured task logging in 3.2.0 multiplying high-volume task runtime by 2.64.

A fix on #62922 shows how much is at stake in a single method. `CommsDecoder.asend`, which every async SDK call of a task goes through (a Variable, a Connection, an XCom, a state store key), made two hops to a worker thread per request; it now makes one. Measured with the benchmarks of this PR, old `comms.py` against new, on the same machine, the middle value of three runs (pytest-codspeed, walltime mode, best time per round):

| Benchmark | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `send`: one sync round trip (code unchanged, the control) | 11.5 µs | 11.4 µs | none |
| `asend`: one async round trip | 108.7 µs | 58.0 µs | **−47%** |
| `asend`: 50 concurrent coroutines on one loop | 18.6 ms | 11.7 ms | **−37%** |

On `main` the benchmarks give the "Before" column; the "After" column is the code of #62922.

An iterated async task makes such calls for every item, so the saving repeats thousands of times per task (the supervisor's and API server's own share of each call is not part of this measurement). The opposite change, an extra thread hop added in passing, would cost as much, and nothing in CI would notice today. A separate ad hoc measurement (4000 `GetVariable` round trips, median of 7 interleaved rounds) agrees: 525 µs to 318 µs per request.

The CI job runs CodSpeed in simulation mode, which counts instructions and leaves system calls (the socket reads and writes, the thread wake-ups) out of the measurement ([CodSpeed docs](https://codspeed.io/docs/instruments/cpu)). So the same change was measured that way too, old `comms.py` and `executor.py` against new, with CodSpeed's own valgrind (3.26.0.codspeed7) and cycle estimation on as in the action, each benchmark in its own process, the middle value of three runs:

| Benchmark | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `send`: one sync round trip (the control) | 106,961 instr. | 107,678 instr. | +0.7% |
| `asend`: one async round trip | 554,228 instr. | 411,956 instr. | **−25.7%** |
| `asend`: 50 concurrent coroutines on one loop | 24.54 M instr. | 16.22 M instr. | **−33.9%** |

Runs of the same code differ by less than 0.7%. Simulation sees a smaller share of the saving than wall time (−26% against −47% for one round trip), because the kernel's part of a thread hop is not counted, but the change is still nearly forty times the run-to-run spread, so CI in simulation mode would flag the reverse change on the PR that makes it.

## What

- `task-sdk/benchmarks/`: a new directory next to `tests/`, for benchmarks only. The first module, `execution_time/test_comms_benchmark.py`, measures one sync round trip, one async round trip and fifty concurrent async round trips against a supervisor thread on a socket pair. The task SDK's pytest configuration only collects `tests/`, so the benchmarks never run with the unit tests. The fake supervisor closes its socket however it ends, so an unexpected request fails the benchmark instead of hanging it.
- A `benchmarks` dependency group in `task-sdk/pyproject.toml` with [pytest-codspeed](https://github.com/CodSpeedHQ/pytest-codspeed) (MIT). Benchmarks are plain pytest functions using its `benchmark` fixture. Locally they run with `uv run --project task-sdk --group benchmarks pytest task-sdk/benchmarks --codspeed`.
- `.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml`: runs them on pushes to `main` and on PRs touching `task-sdk/src/airflow/sdk/execution_time/`, the benchmarks, `task-sdk/pyproject.toml` or `uv.lock`, through `CodSpeedHQ/action` in simulation mode. That mode counts CPU instructions instead of measuring time, so the results do not depend on how busy the shared runner is, and CodSpeed comments each PR with the change against `main`. Every commit on `main` keeps its own run, as the baseline CodSpeed compares PRs with; the job stops after 15 minutes. The action is already on the ASF allow-list (`CodSpeedHQ/action` v5.2.1, pinned by SHA in [apache/infrastructure-actions](https://github.com/apache/infrastructure-actions/blob/main/actions.yml)). It authenticates through OIDC, so no secret is needed for a public repository, but someone with admin rights has to enable the CodSpeed app for `apache/airflow` before the workflow can report anything. Until then the job runs the benchmarks and fails at the upload (`401 Unauthorized`), so the workflow must not be merged before the app is enabled.

## Questions for the dev list

1. **Do we want micro-benchmarks at all?** [AIP-59](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/AIRFLOW/AIP-59+Performance+tests+framework) (Performance tests framework, accepted, still in progress) measures the footprint of whole components: scheduler, workers, triggerer and the database. Micro-benchmarks would be the layer below it, for single methods on hot paths, catching a regression in the PR that introduces it. Is that an extension of AIP-59, or does it need an AIP of its own?
2. **Where should they live and how should they be named?** This draft uses `<distribution>/benchmarks/`, next to `tests/`, with paths that mirror the source module a benchmark covers: `src/airflow/sdk/execution_time/comms.py` is measured by `benchmarks/execution_time/test_comms_benchmark.py`. That mapping is what lets CI run only the benchmarks covering the files a PR changes, instead of the hand-kept path filter the workflow uses in this draft. The `test_*_benchmark.py` names let the existing pytest configuration collect them without changes; a `bench_*.py` convention would need its own `python_files` setting.
3. **Which tool?** pytest-codspeed with the hosted service compares against `main` on each PR, with results that do not depend on runner load. pytest-benchmark is purely local and compares against a saved baseline with a threshold, but wall-time thresholds on shared CI runners are noisy, so they either fail at random or are set too loose to catch a drift.
4. **What should a regression do?** Report only (a PR comment), or fail the check above some threshold?
5. **Which paths come first?** Candidates beyond the comms: XCom serialisation, template rendering, the DAG processor's parsing, and the scheduler's critical section queries.

issue.title: Speed up secret masking of task log lines

repository.name: airflow
repository.description: Apache Airflow - A platform to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor workflows

issue.body:
Every task log line goes through `SecretsMasker.should_hide_value_for_key`, once per key (`dag_id`, `ti_id`, `logger`, ...), and #74840 made it heavier:

```python
def should_hide_value_for_key(self, name):
    if isinstance(name, str) and self.hide_sensitive_var_conn_fields:
        name = name.strip()
        normalized = _NON_WORD_RE.sub("_", name.lower())
        split = _CAMEL_ACRONYM_RE.sub(r"\1_\2", _CAMEL_LOWER_UPPER_RE.sub(r"\1_\2", name))
        split = _NON_WORD_RE.sub("_", split.lower())
        return any(s in normalized or s in split for s in self.sensitive_variables_fields)
```

The answer only depends on the name and the field contents, so it moves into a module-level `lru_cache` keyed by `(name, tuple(sensitive_variables_fields))` — reassigning or mutating the fields can't return a stale answer, and the cache is bounded because variable and connection-extra keys come from user data. `redact_jwt` ran its regex on every string value; strings without `eyJ` now skip it.

In this logging-heavy workload, processing logs in the supervisor creates backpressure on the task, so reducing masking overhead reduces task duration. LocalExecutor, a task writing 100k lines, Linux x86_64; image `apache/airflow:3.4.0b1` with these two files replaced by the versions from main and from this branch. Median of 5 fresh containers per side (each the mean of 2 runs), the two sides run back to back in randomised order:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| BashOperator | 12.5 s | 6.7 s |
| `logging.info` | 12.6 s | 6.7 s |
| `print` | 5.8 s | 3.3 s |

Each of the 5 back-to-back pairs gave a ratio of 0.50–0.54 (Bash), 0.53–0.55 (`logging.info`) and 0.52–0.60 (`print`).

**Tests.** Two new tests cover the cache and the JWT shortcut; both fail if the source change is reverted. Comparing old and new code on 120k key lookups (including in-place edits of the field list) and 100k log events gave identical masking results. An unusual compatibility edge remains: an unhashable `str` subclass used as a name, or an unhashable sensitive-field entry, now raises `TypeError` during cache lookup. `redact` catches this and returns `<redaction-failed>`. Airflow's configuration supplies ordinary strings.

Local: `shared/secrets_masker` 174 passed (1 xfailed), `shared/logging` 111 passed; `test_http_access_log`, `test_decorators` and the OpenLineage redactor tests pass; prek clean. In the four task-sdk modules I ran (`test_log`, `test_operator`, `test_supervisor`, `test_task_runner`), 1075 pass and 11 fail (secrets-backend count and `TriggerDagRun` call assertions); the same 11 failures also occur on the base commit.
